issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma type of witnessed other trauma or with the rest of the profile. 'People cycling' and 'my ex' imply very different personal meanings, and neither has an evident connection to the reported threat items (general unsafety, sleep vigilance, hypervigilance). With only a weak Triggers → Threat link active, the triggers should still plausibly cue the threat state; these two triggers appear idiosyncratic in unrelated directions and are hard to reconcile as part of the same trauma-linked pattern.

vignette:
Omar Haddad was 29 when he came for treatment, a single man of Lebanese American background who had been working as a train conductor for several years. The event he returned to again and again had happened on an early winter shift at an outdoor platform just before dawn. The air had been sharply cold, the kind that stung exposed skin through his uniform collar and gloves. He had been moving along the platform preparing for departure when a man near the edge stumbled during the rush of boarding. Omar did not describe himself as injured, but he had a clear view of what happened next: the body striking metal and concrete, the abrupt shouting, and then the sight of severe visible injuries before emergency crews arrived. What remained with him most vividly was not only the visual shock of blood spreading across the platform, but the combination of that image with the cold biting at his face and hands. He remembered standing there frozen for a moment, feeling the temperature on his skin while taking in wounds he could not make sense of and could not stop looking at.

In the weeks after, Omar noticed that certain moments no longer felt ordinary. On cold mornings at work, when the platform air touched his cheeks in that same cutting way, he would tense immediately. He did not talk about it as a memory at first; instead he would say that something in his body told him to be ready. If a passenger boarded with a bandaged arm, a split lip, stitches above an eyebrow, or any other visible injury, his attention locked there. Seeing blood, even a small amount from a nosebleed or a scraped hand, felt especially hard to tolerate. He would glance away and then look back again, scanning with the uneasy feeling that something terrible could happen at any second. In his mind, safety had become difficult to accept as real. Coworkers might reassure him that a medical issue was under control or that an incident on the platform was minor, but he found it impossible to settle when someone else said things were safe. What mattered to him was that he had once been present for disaster in a place that was supposed to be routine.

At work this took on a particular shape. As a conductor, he spent long stretches on platforms and moving through train cars, always around crowds, doors, edges, and the possibility of accident. He became superalert in a way that others noticed. He watched passengers’ footing, stared at hands gripping railings, tracked anyone who seemed unsteady, and kept checking the platform edge. If he saw a commuter with fresh cuts or blood on clothing, his chest tightened and his concentration narrowed. On especially cold days he dreaded stepping outside between stops because the temperature on his skin pulled him straight back into that winter morning. He did not leave his job, but the strain accumulated. He became more irritable when colleagues brushed off his concern, and he preferred to work without much casual conversation because he was busy scanning.

Nights became difficult in a different but related way. Omar said he had trouble falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert. He did not trust the idea of simply letting go into sleep. Lying in bed, he listened for sounds in the building and kept his attention trained outward, as if vigilance itself were the only responsible position. Even when exhausted, he remained on guard. Friends and relatives told him he was safe at home, that what happened at the station was over, but those words did little for him. He had come to feel that safety was something people claimed, not something that could be relied on. Because of that, rest seemed risky, and he often arrived at work already tired, which only made his alertness feel more necessary.

Over time his world grew narrower without becoming visibly dramatic. He still reported for duty, still carried out the routines of announcements and departures, but he moved through each day as if braced. He avoided looking too directly at injured passengers when he could, yet he also felt unable not to monitor them. He slept less, trusted reassurance less, and felt increasingly alone with the sense that other people did not understand how quickly ordinary scenes could become catastrophic.

What finally brought Omar in was a recent shift during another cold snap when a passenger cut his forehead after slipping on the stairs. The injury was not severe, but Omar saw the blood and felt the winter air hit his face at the same moment, and afterward he found himself unable to calm down even hours later. That night he did not sleep at all. By the time he sought help, what frightened him most was not one single image but the conviction that he could never again believe in safety, no matter who told him otherwise. What he hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to do his job and come home at night without feeling that he had to remain on guard every minute.
